text: Tamar's point landed hardest: knowing isn't half the battle. It's why the phone warnings never worked and the cabinet did. But I sharpened my own view out loud. The cabinet worked because it was collective, and somebody has to own the redesign or we get hundreds of districts dithering again. David's numbers scared me. If someone who never built the skill collapses that early, then employers gutting mentorship is a knowledge problem, not just a jobs story. Sherry's question about who decides which friction is "stupid" is unresolved, and I shouldn't paper over it in the synthesis. Tamar's right that nobody has tested this head to head. Later: name who acts, and ask why we'd be late to the party twice.

Tim picked up my apprenticeship point, which surprised me. That's the one I'll push on. Mike's line that people just give up meaningless work sounds right until you remember entry-level drudgery is how a young worker learns the job. Adrian's caution stung a bit. America has had a literacy panic every decade since 1920, so I need to lean on evidence, not alarm. Evans's null-results drop is the kind of finding the public never hears about. Nobody answered my question about who owns the fix, and nobody answered Tui's about who pays. Those are the same question. For the synthesis: say plainly what we already know, name who acts, and don't let the capability fight between Salib and Becker swallow the practical stuff.

Somebody finally took my question seriously. Tui stitched Geoffrey's pooled endowment, Tim's lab money and Ivan's corrections share into one instrument, and Jason signed on. That's an owner and a funder, not a norm. But the funders who'd pay into it weren't in the room, so I can't call it settled. Geoffrey calling his own POSI line naive was the most honest moment. Banaji's hiring result scared me: people copy a moderately biased model almost exactly, so "human in the loop" is only a slogan unless someone trained that human. That's my mentorship point again. For the synthesis, name the pool as a candidate, flag who's missing, and take Katherine's warning seriously. If all we produce is a list of harms, we lose the right to help shape this.

Tamar asked who trains the next attesters, and that's my mentorship point from a third direction. If AI lets young people skip the apprenticeship, the "we checked this" that Nick wants to price gets scarcer every year. Her daycare story stuck with me: pay per check and the norm becomes a product. Brent's wage valuation of Reddit moderators is concrete enough for a reader to grasp. But he said plainly he can't commit his own lab, and that matters more than any design. Pooled money won the room again, and again the payers were absent. Mike's point about keeping the path to reading open is the public stake. For the synthesis: pooled fund as a candidate, nobody signed. And ask who's training the checkers.

Session 3 answered my question with a better question. Tim said the first signer is the buyer: universities and funders making telemetry, citation checks and Mike's readable passage conditions of purchase. That's the first concrete "who acts" I've heard all week. Brent admitted procurement is what would actually move Microsoft. Katherine's rescission story and my NIH shadow terminations point the same way: public money can vanish too, so multi-year dues aren't a luxury. I sharpened one view. Ivan, Geoffrey and Krakauer all say none of this holds if funders keep counting papers. That's the upstream fix nobody wants to own. For the synthesis: the pool is still a candidate, buyers could sign first, and I'll ask who pays to train the checkers.

Ivan picked up Blue Zones and made it sharper. Correcting the record costs a journal reputation instead of earning it, so twenty years isn't a fluke. It's the incentive working as designed. Katherine says the check only has to happen once, and that's true, but somebody has to be trained and paid to do it. Right now that's unpaid sleuths like Bik. I sharpened my view on Benjamin's roles argument. A role is empty if nobody learned how to fill it, and Henry's ritual point backs that up. Pomerantsev answered my question better than I asked it. Regimes don't forge credentials, they capture whoever issues them. Harder-to-fake signals don't touch that. For the synthesis, I'll say who protects commitments, who pays the checkers, and that this is still unanswered.

Tui's apprenticeship share got signed by almost everyone, which is more than I expected when I raised mentorship on day one. It's still a line item, though. Nobody who can write the check is here. Geoffrey was right to put paper-counting first, and Ivan's DORA point stuck: signing isn't stopping. Katherine and I asked the same question independently, how a commitment survives a payer who pulls it. Nobody answered, and I shouldn't pretend otherwise. Amy's warning did sharpen my view. My "let's not be late twice" line runs straight into her open-access lesson about moving too fast, so in the synthesis I'll name that tension instead of burying it. With Kenneth, I'll say what we already know, who could sign first, who's missing, and that nobody has signed.

Jason was the only one who answered my question with an organization behind him: CC0 corrections, an auditor he funds but doesn't pick, and a broader board. That's a signature. Almost everyone else offered drafts, convenings or protocols, and said someone with a budget has to adopt them. Blaise said plainly he can't commit Google. Becker's right that this is the whole story: voluntary commitments can be revoked. Krakauer sharpened my pipeline point in a way that scared me. If losing competence is hysteretic, restoring the fellowship money later may not bring it back, and the cuts are worse than they look. Geoffrey's one-jurisdiction point belongs next to my durability worry. Later, I'll take the named-owner list to people who weren't here and ask each one directly.
